extracted.intended_audience: scientists and general readers interested in science communication and peer review reform
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and reform criteria for the scientific peer review and publication process (with emphasis on biomedical research), focusing on timeliness, transparency, reviewer selection/expertise, incentives, and post-publication review models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review dual functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Often, peer review is being asked to do two things. It's being asked to look at technical quality and to look at whether an article is suitable for a particular journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and separate these two functions: assessment of methodological/technical rigor versus gatekeeping for journal fit/interest. The article notes peer review may do a reasonable job picking studies of interest to journals but does a poor job of improving paper quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: When researchers make a discovery, it typically takes nine months for them to get the results published in a journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long delays impede rapid communication of scientific results; reform proposals emphasize speeding dissemination (e.g., posting papers publicly before journal peer review) to reduce the nine-month bottleneck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and selection of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The fate of that paper rests on just two or three scientists who have been asked to review it and decide whether it's worthy of being published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on only a few reviewers concentrates influence and increases risk of idiosyncratic or biased decisions; reforms propose broader, community-based review to dilute single-reviewer effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias/conflict risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific reviews may be carried out by someone with a personal axe to grind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to conflicts of interest or adversarial reviewers; transparency of reviews and broader reviewer pools are suggested to mitigate individual biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and ability to evaluate methods/statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers may be unable to truly evaluate a study's methods or statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reviewers have appropriate methodological/statistical expertise; current system sometimes assigns reviewers who cannot detect errors (example: reviewers found only 3 of 9 deliberate errors in test papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of peer review records
rubrics_metrics.description: Make peer reviews and editors' responses available to anyone who wants to understand how a paper was evaluated and chosen for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing reviews and editorial correspondence increases accountability and helps readers judge the evaluation process; transparency is a central reform goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and secrecy as problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews are usually anonymous and kept secret by the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secrecy can hide flaws in the review process and allow unchecked bias; consider publishing reviewer identities or signed reviews, or at minimum making review text public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of peer review to fix experimental design
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists often fail to ask a fundamental question before starting an experiment, which is how many people or animals should be included in a study. By the time a study is done and submitted for publication, it's too late. Peer review is not going to help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address design and power/sample-size issues upstream (e.g., through preregistration, grant/ethics review, or registered reports) rather than relying on post hoc peer review to identify these defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives shaping research behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists are rewarded for getting papers passed peer review in the top journals. That means attention-grabbing findings are valued over careful work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should realign incentives to favor reproducible, durable work rather than flashy results—e.g., continuous post-publication assessment and community valuation rather than journal prestige alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open posting and post-publication (continuous) review
rubrics_metrics.description: Biomedical papers should be posted in public for anyone to see and for peer review to come later; the community of readers can review them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting preprints and allowing ongoing community review (analogous to Amazon product reviews) can expand feedback, increase transparency, and provide sustained assessment over time rather than a single pre-publication gatekeeping event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability of reviews as richer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only thing Amazon ever published were the reviews of the first three people who bought a product, then we'd have a very ineffective system for knowing what was good and bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Amazon-review analogy to argue that broader, public review streams provide more informative and useful feedback than a few anonymous pre-publication reviews; posting reviews online makes evaluation more representative and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoupling technical assessment from journal suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one is to untangle the reasons for peer review in the first place — technical quality vs suitability for a particular journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider separate processes: one for validating technical soundness (which could be open and public) and another for editorial selection about novelty/interest for a journal, reducing conflation of fundamentally different judgments.
